title: GCSE Mathematics (UK)
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public UK GCSE Mathematics specification. Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: A jacket costs £48. In a sale the price is reduced by 25%. What is the sale price of the jacket?
items.explanation: 25% of £48 is £12, so the sale price is £48 − £12 = £36. £12 is only the discount, and the other values do not follow from the price.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: Work out the value of 3/4 + 1/6, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
items.explanation: Rewrite with a common denominator of 12: 9/12 + 2/12 = 11/12. Adding numerators over denominators (4/10) or using a wrong denominator gives the distractors.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: A number is written as 3.6 × 10^4 in standard form. What is its value as an ordinary number?
items.explanation: Multiplying 3.6 by 10^4 moves the digits four places, giving 36000; the other choices place the decimal point after the wrong number of places.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: What is the highest common factor (HCF) of the numbers 84 and 120?
items.explanation: 84 = 2² × 3 × 7 and 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5, so the shared factors give 2² × 3 = 12. 840 is the LCM, and 6 and 24 are not the highest shared factor.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: A bag contains only red, blue and green counters. 40% are red and 25% are blue. What percentage of the counters are green?
items.explanation: The percentages must total 100%, so green is 100% − 40% − 25% = 35%. The other values misread the given percentages or the remainder.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: Work out the value of 2.4 ÷ 0.06, giving your answer as a decimal.
items.explanation: Multiplying both numbers by 100 gives 240 ÷ 6 = 40. Dividing without scaling the divisor produces the smaller distractors.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: Round the number 3.6784 to 2 decimal places.
items.explanation: The third decimal digit is 8, which rounds the second digit 7 up to 8, giving 3.68; truncating gives 3.67 and 3.7 is only one decimal place.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: Write the decimal 0.375 as a fraction in its simplest form.
items.explanation: 0.375 = 375/1000, which cancels by 125 to 3/8. 375/1000 is not in simplest form and 3/4 = 0.75 and 5/8 = 0.625.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: A car travels 180 km in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed in kilometres per hour?
items.explanation: Average speed is distance ÷ time = 180 ÷ 2.5 = 72 km/h; 45 comes from dividing by 4, and 90 from halving 180.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: Work out the value of (2^3 × 2^5) ÷ 2^4.
items.explanation: Add the indices when multiplying and subtract when dividing: 3 + 5 − 4 = 4, so the value is 2^4 = 16; the others misapply the index laws.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: A laptop costing £540 is later sold for £459. What is the percentage loss?
items.explanation: The loss is £540 − £459 = £81, and 81 ÷ 540 × 100 = 15%. The other values use the wrong base or read the loss as a fraction of the sale price.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: Work out the value of 5/8 of 96, giving your answer as a whole number.
items.explanation: One eighth of 96 is 12, so five eighths is 12 × 5 = 60. 48 is half, 72 is three quarters and 80 is five sixths of 96.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: Which of the following numbers is a prime number? Select one option.
items.explanation: 17 has no factors other than 1 and 17. 21 = 3 × 7, 33 = 3 × 11 and 27 = 3 × 9, so each is composite.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: By rounding each number to the nearest whole number, estimate the value of 19.7 × 4.1.
items.explanation: 19.7 rounds to 20 and 4.1 rounds to 4, so the estimate is 20 × 4 = 80; 82 uses an unrounded product and 60 uses 15 × 4.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: Write the decimal 0.75 as a percentage.
items.explanation: To convert a decimal to a percentage multiply by 100, so 0.75 = 75%. The other choices divide by 100 or double the value.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Number

items.stem: Solve the equation 5x − 7 = 23 to find the value of x.
items.explanation: Add 7 to both sides to get 5x = 30, then divide by 5 to give x = 6. The other values come from adding 7 incorrectly or dividing before adding.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: Expand and simplify the expression 3(2x + 5) − 4(x − 2).
items.explanation: 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15 and −4(x − 2) = −4x + 8; combining gives 2x + 23. Sign errors on the second bracket give the other results.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: Factorise fully the expression 6x^2 + 9x.
items.explanation: The highest common factor of 6x^2 and 9x is 3x, giving 3x(2x + 3). The other factorisations are incomplete because a common factor remains inside the bracket.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: The equation of a straight line is y = 3x − 4. What are the gradient and the y-intercept?
items.explanation: In y = mx + c the gradient m is 3 and the y-intercept c is −4, so the line crosses the y-axis at (0, −4); the other options swap or drop the signs.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: Solve the simultaneous equations x + y = 12 and x − y = 4. What is the value of x?
items.explanation: Adding the two equations eliminates y and gives 2x = 16, so x = 8. Subtracting instead gives y, and the other values misread the result.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: Make t the subject of the formula v = u + at.
items.explanation: Subtract u from both sides to get v − u = at, then divide by a, giving t = (v − u) / a. The other rearrangements divide by the wrong quantity.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: Work out the value of 4x^2 when x = −3.
items.explanation: Squaring −3 gives 9, and 4 × 9 = 36. The negative results treat (−3)² as negative, but a square is positive.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: The nth term of a sequence is given by 4n − 3. What is the 10th term?
items.explanation: Substitute n = 10: 4 × 10 − 3 = 37. The value 40 forgets to subtract 3, and the others use the wrong multiple.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: Solve the inequality 3x + 2 < 17 to find the possible values of x.
items.explanation: Subtract 2 to get 3x < 15, then divide by 3 to give x < 5. The other options reverse the inequality sign or divide by 3 incorrectly.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: Expand and simplify the product (x + 4)(x − 3).
items.explanation: Using FOIL: x^2 − 3x + 4x − 12 = x^2 + x − 12. The others come from combining the x terms wrongly or mishandling the constant sign.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: The curve y = x^2 − 2x − 8 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of these points?
items.explanation: Factorising gives (x − 4)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 4 or x = −2. The other pairs do not satisfy the equation.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: A function is given by f(x) = 2x + 1. What is the value of f(−3)?
items.explanation: Substitute −3: 2 × (−3) + 1 = −6 + 1 = −5. Sign errors give −7, and the positive results ignore the negative input.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: Solve the equation x/3 + 2 = 7 to find the value of x.
items.explanation: Subtract 2 to get x/3 = 5, then multiply by 3 to give x = 15. Not multiplying by 3 gives 5, and x = 27 comes from adding 2 instead.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: The expression x^2 − 6x + 5 can be written as (x − p)^2 − q. What are the values of p and q?
items.explanation: Completing the square: x^2 − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)^2 − 9 + 5 = (x − 3)^2 − 4, so p = 3 and q = 4. The other options mishandle the constant.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.stem: A sequence begins 5, 11, 17, 23. What is the nth term of this arithmetic sequence?
items.explanation: The common difference is 6, so the nth term is 6n + c; using the first term, 6(1) + c = 5 gives c = −1, so the nth term is 6n − 1.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Algebra

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: A recipe uses flour and sugar in the ratio 5:2. If 350 g of flour is used, what mass of sugar is needed?
items.explanation: One part is 350 ÷ 5 = 70 g, so the sugar is 70 × 2 = 140 g. 70 g is a single part and 175 g reverses the ratio.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: A map has a scale of 1:25000. Two towns are 6 cm apart on the map. What is the real distance in kilometres?
items.explanation: The real distance is 6 × 25000 = 150000 cm, and 150000 ÷ 100000 = 1.5 km. The other choices misplace the decimal point.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: If 4 identical pens cost £3.20, what is the cost of 7 of these pens?
items.explanation: One pen costs £3.20 ÷ 4 = £0.80, so 7 pens cost 7 × £0.80 = £5.60. The other amounts use the wrong multiplier or divide by 7.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: A loan of £2000 is charged simple interest at 5% per year. How much interest is paid over 3 years?
items.explanation: Simple interest is 2000 × 0.05 × 3 = £300. £100 is one year's interest, and £600 uses a 10% rate.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: An amount of £450 is increased by 8%. What is the new amount?
items.explanation: The multiplier is 1.08, so 450 × 1.08 = £486. £36 is the 8% increase alone and £540 uses a 20% increase.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: Two quantities are in direct proportion. When x = 5, y = 20. What is the value of y when x = 8?
items.explanation: For direct proportion y = kx, so k = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 and y = 4 × 8 = 32. The other values use an incorrect constant of proportionality.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: A car uses 8 litres of fuel to travel 100 km. How many litres are needed to travel 250 km?
items.explanation: Since 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5, the fuel needed is 2.5 × 8 = 20 litres. The other values scale by the wrong factor or divide the distance by the fuel.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: Share £360 between two people in the ratio 5:4. What is the larger share?
items.explanation: There are 5 + 4 = 9 parts, so one part is £360 ÷ 9 = £40; the larger share is 5 × £40 = £200. £160 is the smaller share.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: A population of 5000 increases by 20% each year. What is the population after 2 years?
items.explanation: Using the multiplier 1.2 twice: 5000 × 1.2² = 5000 × 1.44 = 7200. 6000 is only one year's growth, and the others add simple increases.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: The ratio of boys to girls in a school is 3:5. There are 240 boys. How many girls are there?
items.explanation: One part is 240 ÷ 3 = 80, so girls are 80 × 5 = 400. 144 reverses the ratio and 480 adds a further part.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: A jacket is bought for £80 and sold for £92. What is the percentage profit?
items.explanation: Profit is £12, and 12 ÷ 80 × 100 = 15%. 12% forgets to divide by the cost price, and 17.4% divides by the selling price.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: If y is inversely proportional to x, and y = 10 when x = 4, what is y when x = 8?
items.explanation: For inverse proportion y = k/x, so k = 10 × 4 = 40 and y = 40 ÷ 8 = 5. The other values multiply instead of dividing.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: A bank pays compound interest at 4% per year. How much is £500 worth after 2 years?
items.explanation: 500 × 1.04² = 500 × 1.0816 = £540.80. £540.00 uses simple interest, and £541.60 compounds for an extra period.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: Convert a speed of 54 km/h into metres per second.
items.explanation: 54 km/h is 54000 m in 3600 s, so 54000 ÷ 3600 = 15 m/s. The other values divide by the wrong conversion factor.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.domain: Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change
items.stem: A shirt is priced at £40. In a sale the price is reduced by 15%. What is the sale price?
items.explanation: The multiplier is 0.85, so 40 × 0.85 = £34. £6 is the discount alone and £35 subtracts a flat £5.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Ratio, Proportion and Rates of Change

items.stem: A rectangle has a length of 12 cm and a width of 5 cm. What is the length of its diagonal?
items.explanation: By Pythagoras, the diagonal is √(12² + 5²) = √169 = 13 cm. 17 cm adds the sides, and the others do not square correctly.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: The angles in a triangle are in the ratio 2:3:4. What is the size of the largest angle?
items.explanation: There are 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts for 180°, so one part is 20° and the largest angle is 4 × 20° = 80°. The other values are the smaller angles or ignore the ratio.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: A circle has a radius of 7 cm. Using π = 22/7, what is the circumference of the circle?
items.explanation: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 cm. 154 cm is the area (πr²) and 22 cm uses the diameter formula only once.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: What is the mean of the numbers 4, 8, 6, 10 and 7?
items.explanation: The total is 4 + 8 + 6 + 10 + 7 = 35, and 35 ÷ 5 = 7. The other values use the wrong total or divide by the wrong count.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: For the numbers 3, 7, 9, 4, 6 and 8, what is the median?
items.explanation: Ordered, the values are 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9; with an even count the median is the mean of the middle two, (6 + 7) ÷ 2 = 6.5. The others pick a single middle value.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: A triangle has a base of 10 cm and a perpendicular height of 6 cm. What is its area?
items.explanation: Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm². 60 cm² forgets the factor of ½, and 16 cm² adds the dimensions.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: A cuboid measures 3 cm by 4 cm by 5 cm. What is its volume?
items.explanation: Volume = length × width × height = 3 × 4 × 5 = 60 cm³. 47 cm³ adds the dimensions and 12 cm³ multiplies only two of them.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: The probability that a biased coin lands on heads is 0.35. What is the probability that it lands on tails?
items.explanation: Probabilities sum to 1, so tails = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. The other values repeat the heads probability or use an unrelated number.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: In a right-angled triangle the two shorter sides are 6 cm and 8 cm. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
items.explanation: By Pythagoras, the hypotenuse is √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 cm. 14 cm adds the sides and 48 cm multiplies them.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
items.explanation: The numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3. 1/2 counts three outcomes and 2/3 considers all but two.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: What is the mode of the data set 2, 5, 3, 5, 7, 5, 4?
items.explanation: The value 5 appears three times, more than any other, so the mode is 5. The other values are single occurrences or the largest number.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: The exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°. How many sides does the polygon have?
items.explanation: Exterior angles total 360°, so the number of sides is 360 ÷ 24 = 15. The other values divide 360 by a different angle.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue balls. One ball is taken at random. What is the probability that it is red?
items.explanation: There are 8 balls in total and 5 are red, so the probability is 5/8. 3/8 is the probability of blue and 3/5 reverses the ratio.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: For the data set 12, 5, 9, 20, 7, what is the range?
items.explanation: The range is the largest value minus the smallest: 20 − 5 = 15. The other values are the maximum or a single value in the set.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics

items.stem: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. If one angle on the line is 115°, what is the other angle?
items.explanation: The two angles must sum to 180°, so the other is 180° − 115° = 65°. The other values add or subtract from the wrong total.
items.reference: GCSE Maths Specification - Geometry and Statistics
